articles.contentSnippet:
Article URL: https://github.com/xoxorwr/pw-loudness-eq
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50641171
Points: 88
# Comments: 34
articles.fullContent: Windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll. It evens out the volume of each application, so quiet and loud parts play at a similar level. modules/loudness/: the PipeWire module and the DSP plugin. It processes every app's playback stream. modules/limiter/: the output limiter of Windows' audio engine (AudioEng.dll), on every playback device. It keeps the boost from clipping. app/: an optional window (GTK3) to turn it on or off, globally or per app, and set the release time. Install Requires PipeWire ≥ 1.4, and GTK 3 for the window. # Arch: sudo pacman -S pipewire gtk3 pkgconf make gcc # Debian: sudo apt install libpipewire-0.3-dev libspa-0.2-dev libgtk-3-dev pkg-config make gcc make sudo make install systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness, make -C modules/limiter or make -C app. To uninstall, run sudo make uninstall and restart the same services. Usage Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq. The settings live in a PipeWire metadata object, so they can also be scripted: pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 enabled false # turn off pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 release 6 # release time, 2 (fast) to 7 (slow) pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 disabled-apps '["Discord"]' Spa:String:JSON # leave these apps alone pw-metadata -n loudness-eq # show settings Changes apply immediately and are kept across restarts. Configuration Defaults are in /usr/share/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/60-loudness-eq.conf. To override them, copy it to ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/. Arg Default enabled true Start enabled release 4 Windows "Release Time", 2 (fast) to 7 (slow). 4 is the Windows default stream.rules Never process some apps: [ { matches = [ { application.name = "Discord" } ] actions = { loudness-eq = false } } ] Settings changed at runtime are saved in ~/.local/state/pw-loudness-eq/state.conf and take precedence over this file. How it works The loudness module sets audioconvert.filter-graph.90 on each app's playback stream, so the plugin runs inside that stream, before its volume and before mixing, like a Windows stream effect. The limiter module does what Windows' audio engine does on every playback device: after the mix and the software volume, it runs the output through a look-ahead limiter. It's always on, independent of Loudness Equalization, as on Windows. Not processed: JACK clients, streams with more than 8 channels, and Flatpak apps that use PipeWire directly (those going through PulseAudio are processed). The algorithm A broadband automatic gain control. Despite the name, it doesn't equalize the spectrum. Frame size N = 2^⌈log2(fs/100)⌉ (512 at 44.1/48 kHz), with 50% overlap. Each channel is windowed with w[n] = 16384·(1 − cos(2π(n+½)/N)) / (N/2) and run through a real FFT to get the power spectrum. Power is summed into 25 bands with edges at 100, 200, 300, 400, 510, 630, 770, 920, 1080, 1270, 1480, 1720, 2000, 2320, 2700, 3150, 3700, 4400, 5300, 6400, 7700, 9500, 12000, 15500 and 24000 Hz. Channels are summed together. Loudness L = 1.72 · Σ max(E_b − T_b, 1e-32)^0.25, with T = 1000, 100, 31.6, 10, 3.16, 2, 1, 1, .316, .316, 1×11, 4, 10, 100, 1000. Target gain = min((1300/L)^1.6, 10), so at most +20 dB. When the target is lower than the current gain, the gain jumps to it instantly. Otherwise it moves toward it by w = (N/128)·(44100/fs)·0.1^min(r,3)·0.316^(min(r,7)−min(r,3)) per block. At r = 4 that's a time constant of about 4.6 s. The gain is crossfaded linearly across each half-frame. Latency is N samples. The boost can push pure tones such as a whistle well above full scale; the limiter catches that. The limiter Ported from CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dll. audiodg.exe puts it on every render device, after its effects, before the device. articles.fullContent: Anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on. Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care. The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit. I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out. Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type. When you hand a capable model to that engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night. The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards. Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. articles.fullContent: Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.Practical EIP takeoverTo test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want. To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope. TargetsWe wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.Claiming AddressesBy default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:Allocate 25 Elastic IPs in the current region.Store each address, checking for duplicates.Look up each address in the database.Keep and log any address that matches a target’s A record.Release every address that didn’t match.Move to the next region and repeat.In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.The ban hammerAfter 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success. Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. articles.fullContent: By Robert SmithThis post introduces a new algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of \(\pi\) without computing the preceding digits. It beats the standard term-by-term evaluations of Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP), Bellard, and Huvent on operation count. Even against Huvent’s eight-term formula, the savings are about 61% fewer divisions and 38% fewer full modular exponentiations.The key insights come from the following identity:\[ \boxed{ \pi = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\big(2^{1-3k}+2^{-1-5k}\big) + (-1)^k\big(2^{-1-6k}+2^{-4-10k}\big)}{2k+1}. } \]The underlying series goes back to Euler, but has been rearranged to exploit more efficient evaluation. Collecting its terms by odd denominator lets us share the arithmetic in two places:The common denominator \(M=2k+1\) means we can add four remainders and divide once. The surprise is that we don’t have to compute those remainders independently either. The gaps between the exponents are small multiples of \(k\) plus constants, so one starting power and the step \(2^k\bmod M\) let us reach the others by multiplication.Two full exponentiations modulo \(3M\) serve both denominators \(M\) and \(3M\). That gives us up to eight powers of two, and we still only divide once.Together, these two tricks save about a million full exponentiations per million hexadecimal places skipped compared with Huvent, before any machine-specific optimization. In practice, this algorithm leads to an implementation that runs in nearly 40% less wall-clock time.The BBP trick and formula convergenceTo see where the savings come from, let’s recall the BBP trick. To skip \(n\) hex digits, shift \(\pi\) left by \(d=4n\) bits and take the fractional part. Shifting by \(d\) bits adds \(d\) to each exponent, so we’re left adding and subtracting terms of the form \(2^E/N\). When \(E\ge 0\), write \(2^E=qN+r\). Then \(2^E/N=q+r/N\), and we don’t care about \(q\): it’s an integer. Even at \(d=4{,}000{,}000\), we can compute \(r=2^E\bmod N\) without ever constructing a four-million-bit numerator.The terms with \(E<0\) make up the tail. They decay geometrically, so we sum them directly, keeping enough guard bits to settle the last digit we want.The above is essentially the BBP trick, and is the basis for three decades of digit extraction algorithms.As such, when I was programmatically looking for efficient BBP-formula, I ranked them by how many fractions I’d have to evaluate to reach a given digit. Each fraction in the main loop costs me a modular exponentiation and a division. Bellard’s formula advances 10 bits for every seven fractions; Huvent’s formula advances 12 bits for every eight. After finding Huvent’s formula independently, I’ve tried feverishly to find one with a better ratio, without success. So I looked toward ways of optimizing existing series.One clue tipped me off. There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s terse derivation. He has one sum in powers of \(1/4\) and another in powers of \(1/1024\). Since \(4^5=1024\), splitting the first sum into five progressions lets him write both sums in powers of \(1/1024\). What if, instead of lining up the powers, we lined up the denominators?Lining up denominatorsLining up denominators seemed hard with the many-term series of Bellard and Huvent. articles.fullContent: Who needs a GPU? In my work at Bevyl I was really impressed by the performance and cost characteristics of AWS Lambdas. They can massively distribute and fan out CPU-bound work, which is amazing for things like ffmpeg on long videos. So I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. It was a random idea built on a hunch, and I like to prove such ideas right or wrong by building. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson! I picked H2O-Lightning, a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B, because I wanted a small model built for decisions. I figured if this architecture had any legs, only doing decision models (a single forward pass) is the move. A decision model reads a document and answers a question about it by picking one option. Fanning out So the trick, if it's possible, would be fanning out. I was inspired how Remotion uses massively parallelized Lambdas to render videos. I wanted to prove this was possible to do, so I kept a constraint of a 3 GB limit for Lambdas. The whole model is 9.3 GB, so it does not fit in one. But it has 32 layers of about 225 MB each, and one layer fits. That gave me one Lambda job per layer per block of tokens. Think of the Lambda as a simple idempotent API. A job reads inputs from S3, does the math, and writes one object back. x = load(f"{doc}/{layer - 1}/{block}") memory = load(f"{doc}/{layer}/{block - 1}") y, memory = model.layers[layer](x, memory) s3.put_object( Key=f"{doc}/{layer}/{block}", Body=pack(y, memory), ) Each job waits on the layer above for the same block and on its own previous block. Each layer starts one step after the layer above it, like a staircase 32 layers deep. 92% of the work parallelizes, 8% is serialhoped it couldbe done hereactually done herelayer 1layer 2layer 3layer 4layer 5waiting its turntimeParallel but not. I'm proud of the win: splitting a model call across 5,600 Lambdas is kinda wild. One request, 32 layers, 5,600 Lambda invocationsLambda job that has to run in orderLambda job that can run any timePoint at a job to follow its block.0 s5 s10 s15 sseconds after the read startslayer 1layer 8layer 16layer 24layer 32Win: the math worked; I had split a model call into 5,600 Lambda invocations.Fail: 17 seconds to read ~4k tokens. The bill If it was 40x slower but 50% cheaper, that'd be interesting. Reading a 4,000-token document takes 17 seconds and costs 3.4 cents. That works out to $8.40 per million tokens. Google sells a hosted decision model, Gemini Decision 1, for $0.10 per million tokens, so the same read costs 0.04 cents there. Mine is more than 80 times more expensive. articles.fullContent: Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most important theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).” Can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts. FACT 0: GDP per person correlates with good things What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’. In richer countries, on average people are happier. Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer: Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die: Are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less: More intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more: Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person: And all of this is correlation not causation. But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing. Which brings us to: FACT 1: Everyone used to be poor This is the most important fact about human history. We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth. Everyone used to be poor. This is the most important fact about macro history. Why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape: FACT 1b: Wages were stagnant before the Industrial Revolution This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250. Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence. We lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until: FACT 2: Growth accelerated with the Industrial Revolution The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in human history. We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate. articles.fullContent: Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction. More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS. Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use. How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip. Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction. High Refresh Rate Interactions Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area. If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor. In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations. Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed. Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region. Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container. Want a dial with notches? Snap points! The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough. Creating “The Controller” I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless. Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously. First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core. Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website. What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval. articles.fullContent: july 23, 2025 my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format. lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]]. however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]). the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===], not with a ]] or a ]==], or a ]====]. here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it: local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q, but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code. anyway, download this file. if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose. design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use. styles of data representation JSON style (LON?) chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program. return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead. return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead. articles.fullContent: A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson. Left. One phrase in the hands of 21 writers who were held out of training. The model read one to three real words by each of them and carried on in their hand. Right. Drawings from typed prompts. I picked these by eye from the best third of the samples; there are unpicked ones further down. The text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I plan to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall. Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad. So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt. Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected. How it works The whole recipe. Pen points snap to a grid (b) so a word becomes a walk in eight directions plus pen-down and pen-up. Byte-pair encoding merges common runs of moves into tokens (c): this "world" goes from 156 moves to 47 tokens. Everything else is a plain decoder that cross-attends to what it's told. That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture. The data Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive. The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them. Every writer the model knows, saying hello. Each one is placed by its learned vector, with print on the left and cursive on the right. Nobody told the model which was which. Color is the source the pages came from. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. articles.fullContent: A network with 2 layers and about 5 million weights solves 87% of a test set of extremely hard Sudokus. DeepSeek R1, o3-mini-high, and Claude 3.7 solve none of them. It’s an unfair fight, since the little one has never seen anything but Sudoku. Still, its trick is now inside language models you can download. It runs the same few layers over and over. Here’s that trick on an easy puzzle. Both grids follow one rule, where an empty cell gets a number only if that number is the only one that fits. The left grid gets three passes, like a model with three layers. The right one gets to keep going. stack537619598686348317266284195879after 0 of 3 passes30 of 81loop537619598686348317266284195879after 0 passes30 of 81Same puzzle, same rule. The stack gets 3 passes, and the loop keeps going. The grid on the right never got any smarter. It just got more turns. Last week, Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model small enough to run on a 32GB MacBook, and its launch post says it runs “the middle layers of the model three times for every token.” Three days later, Z.ai said its new flagship, GLM-5.4, does the same thing at a much bigger size, running 28 of its layers twice. That’s two labs in one week, for an idea that’s been kicking around since 2018. Running the same layers twice sounds a bit like rereading a page you just read, since the weights don’t change between passes. So where does the second pass find anything new? And if it helps that much, why isn’t every model doing it? I’m going to answer both with one Sudoku, the one from that race, and you get to play it as we go. Then we’ll follow it into how Inkling 2 Mini is actually wired, what its extra passes buy on benchmarks, and the bill they run up on your GPU. 1) One rule, many passes Nobody solves a Sudoku in one look. You scan the grid, fill in whatever you’re sure of, and scan again, and the second scan finds more because the first one filled things in. This is that process on the puzzle from the race, the example from Wikipedia’s Sudoku page, except this time you’re the one pressing the loop button. Each press runs one pass. You can also tap a cell and fill it in yourself when you see something the rule missed. (It’s a pretty dumb rule, so you probably will.) Wikipedia's example puzzlebefore any pass30 of 81 filledRun a pass, or fill a cell yourself. Bold numbers are the clues. Notice what stayed the same. The rule is identical on every pass, so pass 7 is no cleverer than pass 1. It finds numbers pass 1 couldn’t because the grid in front of it has changed. The stack in the race got three of these passes and then had to stop, and a normal model is stuck in exactly that spot. 2) A normal model, in Sudoku terms Why does a normal model only get three? Well, it gets its scans from its layers, and it has a fixed number of those. A language model is a stack of layers. Your text goes in as tokens, each token becomes a list of a few thousand numbers, and that list climbs the stack, through layer 1, then layer 2, and on up to the top. Llama 3 8B has 32 layers. Inkling 2 Small, the bigger model Thinking Machines released earlier this month (and the one I first assumed was the looped one), has 48. Each layer has its own weights, the numbers the model learned in training. Its attention part lets the token pull in information from the tokens before it, and its MLP part runs the token’s numbers through a few big multiplications on their own. Then the layer adds its result onto the list instead of replacing it (that’s a residual connection), so every layer makes a small edit and hands the list up. Back in Sudoku terms, every layer is a different person with a different checklist, and each one gets exactly one look at the grid. The word “the” and the last word of a hard question get the same number of looks. And once a token’s numbers leave layer 10, nothing ever sends them back. For an easy puzzle, that’s plenty. For a hard one, the model can run out of looks before it run

articles.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
articles.contentSnippet: Huang still faces questions from Congress and his own board about his romantic relationship with an alleged chip smuggler.
articles.fullContent: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company confronts. The chipmaker still faces multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of US export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up, and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. US Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities & Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The US government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and re-sellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the US government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from US trade due to national security concerns. The US also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase US chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the US government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China, and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. articles.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
articles.contentSnippet: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.
articles.fullContent: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media. The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported, citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy. Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings. Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman. “When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.” Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however. articles.fullContent: After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man. Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
articles.contentSnippet: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.
articles.fullContent: AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives. According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences. ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them. The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots, and Claude Duet, respectively. In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs. Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are. ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems. It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time. For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust. Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time. The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request. While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions. While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested

articles.title: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
articles.contentSnippet: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
articles.fullContent: Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent. The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work. The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea. Image Credits:Walmart To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart. Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent. Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to. The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store. Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant. Beyond Muse, Walmart has recently rolled out more AI-powered features to its own shopping assistant, Sparky. Some of the newer additions include turning handwritten shopping lists into shopping carts, using photos and voice commands to find products, and helping customers get around their local store. Shoppers can search for an item and use a pin on the store map to see exactly which aisle it’s in. There’s also a “Flash Price Tag” button that makes the item’s shelf label light up. articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
articles.contentSnippet: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.
articles.fullContent: As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple, co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself. “We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman. “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.” “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds. The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies and data collection practices, and sometimes even training on users’ personal data. Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place. Image Credits:Maple.ai Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work, offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled. With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and other AI agents that work over chat. articles.title: Dozens of oil and shipping tankers hacked in recent weeks, per report
articles.contentSnippet: Iran is the chief suspect behind the dozens of cyberattacks targeting oil and chemical shipping vessels.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 1:09 PM PST · November 24, 2026 Image Credits:Tom Pennington / Getty Images U.S. officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks targeting shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. The ships carrying oil, liquefied gas, and other explosive chemicals were hacked as they traveled across Asia and Europe. Several oil tankers headed toward the U.S. coast in August also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cybersecurity teams within the FBI and Coast Guard to board the vessels. The report said officials are investigating if Iran is expanding its recent wave of hacks against the U.S. by targeting large vessels to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or to cause an explosion at a port. (Ships have backup controls in the event that automated systems are hacked or fail.) Hackers may have been abusing a bug dubbed FortiBleed, which allows hackers to break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet-made routers. A joint FBI-Coast Guard security alert from September warned that Fortinet routers are used on shipping vessels. Iran has been firing back on all sides since the start of the U.S./Israel-led war earlier this year, which killed the country’s supreme leader. Many of Iran’s retaliations have been in the form of cyberattacks, with U.S. officials blaming Iran for hacks targeting hundreds of American water providers and U.S. medical tech companies. A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the shipping hacks or whether it had a more accurate figure. articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups

articles.fullContent: Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close. Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value. The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector. The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies. Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. articles.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
articles.contentSnippet: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.
articles.fullContent: The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks. The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post. The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed. The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds. While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices. “Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote. The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data. The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.” The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes. articles.title: Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags
articles.contentSnippet: The addition of live stock quotes and charts could help Threads attract the financial community that has historically relied on X.
articles.fullContent: It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags. While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively. Image Credits:screenshot of Threads on iPad The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock. In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them. The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X. Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time. articles.fullContent: Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs. The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content. Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes. Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app. Image Credits:Meta Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore. Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected. Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada. articles.title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
articles.contentSnippet: The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.
articles.fullContent: Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision. Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI. The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated. The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures. Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X. A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done…— rsa (@rsa) November 24, 2026 The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams. “It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried,” the company said in a post. Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%. articles.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
articles.contentSnippet: Next-generation data centers will need tens of gigawatts of power every year. One of Crusoe's investors thinks solar and energy storage are the obvious choice.
articles.fullContent: The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year. “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.” It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster. That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market. “Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.” Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said. G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said. The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage. “The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.” In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly. Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now. “It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said. articles.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
articles.contentSnippet: While other social platforms have focused on restricting teens' access to AI chatbots, Pinterest is addressing the AI content filling their feeds.
articles.fullContent: Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play. Image Credits:Pinterest The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience. Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback. WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions. But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls. This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18. Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled. Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app. The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. articles.title: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the silicon gap with Nvidia
articles.contentSnippet: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart for a reported $7.5 billion is part of its efforts to improve the efficiency of its Trainium chips.
articles.fullContent: Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion. The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer. Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips. By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business. In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to. One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path. Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago. In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.” Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.fullContent: The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.What material is the Army planning to detonate?There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.“It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.Why is the Army detonating it now?Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”What are the risks?Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretar
